claims.text: Conventionally infiltrated or sintered W–Cu composites typically suffer from phase separation and void-related defects.
Phase separation and voids degrade thermal transport and mechanical performance in W–Cu composites.
A thin, uniform Ni interlayer should be vapor-deposited onto W surfaces before Cu infiltration or matrix processing.
The proposed processing will produce a coherent Ni interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
A Ni interlayer improves wetting between W and Cu.
A Ni interlayer improves diffusion bonding at the W–Cu interface.
Ni lowers the interfacial energy between W and Cu.
The Ni coating promotes uniform Cu wetting and interdiffusion at W–Cu interfaces.
The Ni transition layer inhibits void formation during subsequent processing.
The Ni transition layer inhibits phase separation during processing and irradiation service.
Ni-coated W–Cu will have fewer critical voids and defective phase contacts than an otherwise identical uncoated W–Cu composite.
Ni-coated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than W–Cu made by standard infiltration or sintering without an interlayer.
Ni-coated W–Cu will retain greater mechanical integrity after fusion-relevant irradiation and thermal cycling than the uncoated baseline.
Reduced interfacial defects will produce superior heat-transfer performance and mechanical durability under irradiation.
Analogous refractory-material evidence supports improved interfacial bonding from the proposed intervention.

contradictions.description: The initial state and boundary describe W regions as already embedded within a Cu matrix, whereas the intervention requires exposed W surfaces to be vapor-coated before Cu matrix processing. The fabrication sequence is therefore internally ambiguous unless the intended starting state is a bare W preform rather than an already formed W–Cu composite.
